#8638. A Frightening Encounter on a Dark Road Nearly Took Night Running From Me. This Year, I’m Taking It Back.

I N THE DARK, the headlights cast a distorted version of my silhouette on the industrial building to my left as the vehicle makes its way past me. I’m running along an otherwise desolate road, not far from my house. The car comes to a halt at the stop sign about 300 feet in front of me—and idles. My legs instinctively slow down, my body reacting before my mind has a chance to catch up. I quickly calculate what to do next. There are no side streets I can turn into—I either have to run past the car or turn around, which would add a few miles to my run that I’m not ready for. Maybe the driver is just checking his phone, I tell myself.

But the broad-shouldered man with a long graying beard at the wheel is waiting for me with the window rolled down, his arm resting in its frame. He starts shouting before I can make sense of the situation: What do I think I am doing, running in the dark? Am I trying to get killed? My body tenses, anticipating the man’s possible next move. He has daughters my age, he continues, and he’d kill them if they did that. Could I at least carry this with me, he roars, throwing a key-chain alarm to my feet, then driving off before I have a chance to react.

I sprint the last half a mile home, propelled by anxious energy. My inability to focus only fuels my confusion; so does the blue egg-shaped alarm in my trembling hand that I don’t have a clear memory of picking up but am holding nevertheless. I try to replay in my head how it got there—and why. I have reflective bands on both my arms and my ankles, so drivers can spot me. I use my phone’s light to illuminate the ground in front of me whenever I need to.

The next day, I don’t run outside in the dark. Too cold, I convince myself when I step on the treadmill I hate so much in my apartment complex gym. Too rattled, is what I am unwilling to admit. Because do I have any right to feel that way when technically nothing happened to me? The stranger, in the end, didn’t hurt me.

Still, something changed on the road in the dark.

With every rhythmic thump the belt makes, I am less determined to keep going. My mind can’t handle the monotony. I start skipping days when I cannot make it out for a daytime run. At some point over the next few weeks, the key to the gym falls behind the shoe rack, and I don’t even notice.

THE LIKELY DIAGNOSIS is seasonal affective disorder. It could also be winter blues, but that one is milder and more temporary. My somber mood and low energy seem constant. For most people, it passes by spring, my therapist says. What helps? For one, exercise! But at that point, my couch’s cushions have resigned to accepting my body’s indentation as their new shape.

By the time spring comes, my fitness is at odds with my enthusiasm for the prolonged daylight, and I end up with shin splints. I spend the rest of the year trying to heal and return to form.

I don’t forget about the gray-bearded man. In fact, I share the story, framing it as a silly encounter. “Would you believe that?” I say with a forced smile.

“That’s not okay,” my friends and coworkers answer with their words as much as their faces.

My feelings start morphing from self-blame into anger. What should have been clear to me from the beginning dawns on me slowly: Vigilance is important, but the solution to a stranger’s concerns about my safety is not to instill more fear in the name of “protection.” Women running at night are not the problem. We’ve long ago dismantled the patriarchal notion that men should be our protectors when, in fact, they often pose the danger.

And so when the clock falls back an hour at the start of November, I’m determined not to fall back into a cycle of seasonal depression and injury.

BY MID-DECEMBER, it’s dark by 4:30 p.m. I wrap my torso in color-changing LED tubes. Today I pick emerald. As I descend the trail that clings to the bank of the Delaware River, the historic cantilever bridge that crosses the water comes into view, itself wrapped in green color-changing lights. I smile for no other reason but that we match.

I run up a semicircle road where, for a moment, the world is reduced to cones of warm yellow glowing from vintage streetlights. My chest lamp illuminates just enough ground in front of me to fit my next two steps. Beyond that, I trust that my feet remember what my eyes cannot see.

The darkness has a way of taming my unruly mind. The stillness mutes my whirling thoughts, a nearly impossible achievement among the hectic noise of daylight. It’s the closest I come to meditating, to understanding what it means to be present. It doesn’t matter where the road leads or how long is left of my run; it’s only here and now. The quiet is mostly disrupted by my own two feet. They take turns striking the ground, but their thuds meet in the echo that reverberates off building walls before getting swallowed up by the endless nightfall blue encircling me.

How did I ever allow this to be taken away from me?

Someone lingers at the end of the sidewalk in front of me, and I instinctively switch to the opposite side, picking up speed.

The person pays me no mind, looking in the direction of a leash they’re holding, the end of which I cannot make out. The black road becomes deserted again, and I slow my pace. What was born out of necessity has grown into my favorite part of the day. I love this. I need this. This is the world I want to live in.

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2026 issue of Runner’s World.

Pavlína Černá, an RRCA-certified run coach and cycling enthusiast, has been with Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Popular Mechanics since August 2021. When she doesn’t edit, she writes; when she doesn’t write, she reads or translates. In whatever time she has left, you can find her outside running, riding, or roller-skating to the beat of one of the many audiobooks on her TBL list.

#8637. The Best Smith Machine for Your Home Gym in 2025

The Smith machine sometimes gets a bad rap, but it can be a solid addition to any home gym.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Nov 2, 2026

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Other than the almighty treadmill, there may not be a piece of equipment more synonymous with commercial gyms than the Smith machine. Boasting tremendous versatility and functionality, this muscle-building tool is popular among lifters of all experience levels.

However, you don’t need a gym membership to enjoy its benefits. While it may have not been a home gym staple years ago, the Smith machine has become a must-have for many fitness enthusiasts. Offering added protection without a spotter for your bench presses, back squats, deadlifts, and other strength exercises, the Smith machine is a wise investment for those trying to build the ultimate garage gym.

With options spanning from traditional Smith machines to all-in-one home gym solutions, you might feel a bit overwhelmed about which direction to go. Luckily for you, our team of expert product testers did all the due diligence necessary to separate the cream from the crop. From analyzing the build materials to testing the smoothness of the bar path to assessing the value, we took the time to dissect each element in order to narrow down our list to just five.

In addition, we got some valuable insight from Mauro S. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness, on the benefits and what factors to consider when you’re shopping for a Smith machine.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If you’re searching for a multifunctional Smith machine that’s compatible with a ton of attachments, the Force USA G15 is the machine that can truly do it all — albeit at an expensive price point of around $5,500. However, there’s a reason it earned 4.5 out of 5 stars for versatility from our top product tester: you can perform a wide variety of exercises by taking advantage of all of its functionality.

Tipping the scales at nearly 1,000 pounds, the G15 combines a functional trainer, half rack, and Smith machine into a single, sturdy unit. Measuring over 6 feet wide, over 4 feet deep, and about 7 feet tall, the G15 earns a 4-star footprint rating. While there are more compact options, it’s still a good option for folks with limited space, especially considering the versatility you get.

Offering dual 289-pound weight stacks that keep it well-anchored, the G15 also scores 4 out of 5 stars for durability and construction.

“This thing is like a tank,” our tester says. “Once it’s assembled, it’ll basically be stuck in place.”

Unfortunately, our tester wasn’t as impressed with the cable pulley material. Asthey’re made from nylon instead of aluminum, they don’t move as smoothly and won’t be as durable as their metal counterparts.

Something that separates the G15 from many competitors is its ability to go from a 2:1 or 4:1 pulley ratio. This gives you the ability to make the weight feel like half or a quarter of the actual weight. While our tester would prefer a 1:1 ratio for more effective resistance, he says the 2:1 or 4:1 ratios “will be adequate for most people working out from home.”

The G15 comes with a lengthy list of attachments, including J-hooks, safety spotter arms, multi-grip dip handles, a multi-grip pull-up bar, band pegs, and a low row footplate. If you want to unlock even more training possibilities, the $700 G15 Upgrade Kit includes three additional strength training stations, three functional attachments, a TV mount, and four storage shelves.

Two knocks against this ultra-versatile machine: assembly and value.

Although some of the parts arrive pre-assembled, our assembly expert recommends budgeting “at least 20 man hours” to get the G15 fully put together. And if you want to leave it to the professionals, you’ll need to pay an additional $800.

At nearly $6,000 on its own, the G15 certainly isn’t made for budget-conscious shoppers. Our top product tester gave it 3.5 out of 5 stars for value, noting that Force USA could use better quality components, cables, and accessories, including one of the key parts of this premium-priced unit: the built-in barbell.“The knurling is super passive and not going to allow for an adequate grip for the user if you were to go heavy on any Smith machine movements,” he explains.

Want to crush a full-body workout with a single piece of equipment? The Titan Fitness Smith Machine can be the all-in-one solution that allows you to train your upper body, lower body, and core in a safe, effective manner.

Is it as versatile as the G15? No. Is it far more affordable? Yes.

For less than a third of the price, you can still get an excellent workout experience from the $1,7000 Titan Smith Machine. One of our more seasoned product testers used it for a variety of strength training sessions, highlighting how impressed she was by the smooth glide of the barbell and the angled design. In addition, this Smith machine is counterbalanced so you don’t have to support the entire 45-pound barbell like you do on other machines. Beginners will appreciate this, as the bar only feels like 15 pounds.

Unfortunately, like Force USA, Titan left our team wanting more out of the knurling.

“It’s fine for a Smith machine, but it’s definitely not the most grippy bar,” our tester says.

On the other hand, this machine earns high marks for its ergonomics. Our tester rated it 4 out of 5 stars in this category. She found the single-axis, angled design helped improve her muscle activation during lower-body weight training exercises like Smith machine squats and lunges.

Most importantly, she felt completely secure using this Titan machine. Not only was there no wobbling or shaking, but the bar moved smoothly, leading her to give a 5-out-of-5 rating for stability.

“This is a super stable machine; there was no give to it even when we were using heavy weights,” our tester says. “This was ultra-smooth.” While Titan priced this machine fairly, we’d like to see a better warranty. A one-year policy falls well short of what we expect from most brands. Plus, if you want to return a piece of equipment, you must pay the return shipping costs and a 20% restocking fee. That results in a disappointing customer experience score of just 2 out of 5 stars.

Don’t want a standalone Smith machine? Bolt Fitness has a space-saving solution in the form of the Storm Series Stinger Smith Machine Attachment. Compatible with any 3” x 3” frame using 1” hardware, this universal attachment can seamlessly integrate with your existing squat or power rack, opening the door to even more training possibilities.

We rate this Smith machine attachment a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers 12 different positions totaling 60” of vertical adjustments. That means you can quickly go from a steep incline bench press to a Romanian deadlift, making your workouts more efficient, too. Plus, we also like that this attachment has a 43” built-in multi-grip pull-up bar, giving you the ability to develop your vertical pulling strength and endurance.

Bolt also earns solid marks for construction, earning 4 out of 5 stars in this key category. However, our chief product tester warns not to expect quite the same level of craftsmanship as some better-known brands.

“You won’t see the same quality welds or powder coats from Bolt as you will from Rogue or REP,” he says.

Like several other nominees on this list, our tester was also disappointed with the Smith bar’s knurling. The passive knurl pattern won’t give you a particularly stable grip, especially when using heavier weights.

“You definitely won’t mistake this for an Olympic barbell,” our tester says.

As for the price? At around $1,100 this is on the expensive side for a Smith machine attachment. For example, the Bells of Steel Smith Machine Rack Attachment is much more affordable at $800. We rate it a 3 out of 5 for value, especially since you already need a rack to use it. Otherwise, expect to invest a significant chunk of change to get a fully functioning setup.

Just because you can’t afford to splurge on something like the G15 doesn’t mean you can’t find a Smith machine that fits within your budget. If you don’t have a ton of financial wiggle room, the RitFit Smith Machine is the most affordable option that earned our stamp of approval.

As our top product tester puts it, “If you’re looking for a Smith machine and you’re on an ultra-budget, this is it.”

At about $500 on Amazon, this machine is less than a third of the price of the Titan Fitness Smith Machine and less than a tenth of the cost of the G15. Of course, it’s not the most durable option on the market, but it offers sufficient versatility at a very attractive price point to earn a near-perfect value rating of 4.5 out of 5 stars.

Dubbed the “sleeper pick” by our tester, he notes that “the low price covers so many sins.”

Before we dive into some of RitFit’s shortcomings, let’s highlight some of the strengths of this machine. First, we rated it 4 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers built-in low row and lat pulldown capabilities using a plate-loaded cable pulley system that holds 165 pounds. The RitFit Smith Machine also comes with several attachments, including a pin-on landmine row and two multi-purpose pull-up handles.

Secondly, it has a compact design that makes it suitable for home gym setups with limited  space. It also weighs just 140 pounds, making it easier to move than other options on this list.

However, our tester had several callouts about the RitFit Smith Machine that deserve mentioning. With cheaper build materials and a lightweight design, it didn’t prove to be as stable as he would have liked, earning just 3.5 out of 5 stars for both construction and stability. Needless to say, this isn’t the best option if you want to lift heavy weights. Still, considering you could pay around the same price for a high-quality Olympic barbell, the RitFit Smith Machine is a solid option if you’re on a limited budget.

Imagine if you could turn your squat rack into a Smith machine in a matter of minutes. That dream can be a reality if you’re willing to invest around $700 on the VTS Lite Rack Attachment from Bulletproof Fitness, a lesser-known fitness equipment manufacturer that’s caught our attention.

While we haven’t gotten our hands on this attachment just yet, it’s hard not to get excited about the concept and execution by Bulletproof. The Versa Trolley System (VTS) Lite allows you to convert your squat rack into a Smith machine using your own barbell. The rollers are made from UHMW plastic, an ultra-durable material we’ve seen used on other racks. This attachment only weighs 15 pounds, making the VHS Lite a more user-friendly alternative than the full-sized VTS, which weighs in at 24 pounds. From a construction standpoint, we feel comfortable giving the VTS Lite 4 out of 5 stars.

In addition, we like that Bulletproof offers a wide range of options to accommodate different racks. You can choose between a 3” x 3” pair, a 2” x 3” pair, or a 2” x 2” pair. You also can choose different hook sizes based on the diameter of your barbell. This optionality, along with the added exercise variety you get from using the attachments, earns a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility.

Set to be released in May 2025, we’re excited to see this product in action. If you want a more streamlined solution than getting a standalone Smith machine, this is an attractive space- and money-saving solution. Based on the price and versatility, we give it a value rating of 4 out of 5 — though it could go higher once we get our hands on it.

As Smith machines have become more popular among the home gym community, we’ve ramped up our efforts to test ones from a variety of brands. This has allowed us to develop a thorough evaluation process that examines a number of key factors that impact your workout experience.

With options ranging from standard Smith machines to all-in-one trainers with cable machines, here’s what we assess during testing using a 1-5 scoring system:

What makes a Smith machine such a valuable training tool? If you’ve ever used one, you already know there’s added peace of mind knowing you have built-in support. Here’s an overview of the different benefits of utilizing this popular piece of equipment.

Unlike when you use a barbell and squat rack, the Smith machine provides a fixed bar path. This can help reduce the risk of injury and ensure a stable lifting environment.

“The Smith machine helps the athlete feel supported and gives them greater control and stability when performing an exercise,” says Mauro M. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness.

In particular, new lifters can benefit from starting out on a Smith machine so they can focus on their form while being supported by the machine.

“Maintaining correct form is important for avoiding injuries and maximizing the effectiveness of your workouts,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, PhD, RD. “Beginners might benefit from working with a personal trainer initially or taking a beginner class to learn proper techniques.”

The guided motion and added stability of a Smith machine makes it an ideal training tool for those returning from injury or anyone with mobility issues. It encourages proper form and can be a safer way to increase your strength and joint stability before moving on to free weights.

Maietta recommends starting with lighter weights to get a feel for the range of motion before progressing. “The fixed range of motion is not for everyone, so be sure to speak with your local fitness professional and listen to your body and joints if you feel any discomfort or pain during the planned movements,” he says.

If you prefer to work out alone or don’t have a training partner available, the Smith machine can act as a “spotter” for you. These machines offer an extra layer of safety, as you can easily rack the bar or set the safety spotters to a specific point that will keep you out of harm’s way.

In addition, this advantage allows you to safely follow progressive overload, a proven method for increasing muscle size and strength.

“This continual challenge helps your muscles grow stronger,” says Mohr. “It’s important to start with manageable increments to prevent injury.”

You won’t find many machines that offer as much versatility as the Smith machine. Want to train legs? You can knock out squat and lunge variations. Want to grow your chest and shoulders? Grab an adjustable weight bench and work on your bench press and overhead press without having to worry about keeping the bar stable. A high-end option like the Force USA G15 gives you the ability to perform cable exercises like cable crossovers, chest flys, and overhead triceps extensions.

“The Smith machine can be seen as the Swiss army knife of the weight room since it allows for several strength training exercises in its fixed vertical path, ranging from squats to overhead pressing movements,” says Maietta.

What should you consider when choosing a Smith machine? Based on our experience as equipment experts and dedicated lifters, here’s what we recommend:

Consider the machine’s footprint when determining if it is a good fit for your needs. One benefit of Smith machines is all-in-one trainers are available to consolidate the space needed for multiple workout stations.

Many of the home gym Smith machine options on this list are designed as all-in-one trainers designed to provide multiple workout functions with one convenient machine. The machine can include stations for a power rack, functional trainer, low-row attachment, chin-ups/pull-ups, dips, suspension trainers, and more.

Smith machines offer pulley systems with varying weight ratios, including 1:1 and 2:1. A 1:1 ratio means the weight you load is the exact weight you lift. A 2:1 ratio means you lift half of the weight you load. For instance, with a 2:1 ratio, if you load 100 pounds, you lift 50 pounds.

Some Force USA Smith machines, including the G15, allow users to easily switch between 2:1 and 4:1 ratios, which is helpful when people of various skills use the same machine.

Weight capacities vary depending on the functions offered by the machine. The weight capacities on this list start at 300 pounds. Be sure to confirm the machine’s weight capacity can accommodate your needs..

If you are looking for versatile strength-building home gym equipment to achieve a full-body workout, a Smith machine can help you achieve your goals. Since the 1950s, this game-changing machine has allowed gym-goers to work out safely without a spotter. Today, there is a wide range of consumer options, allowing you to experience the benefits of the Smith machine in the comfort of your own home gym.

Smith machines all perform similar functions, but there are different types of Smith machines available. For instance, some Smith machines provide a vertical path for motion, while other Smith machines provide a slightly angled path. Some Smith machines may be limited to the Smith machine function, while others are designed to be all-in-one machines with multiple stations for different exercises. Smith machines vary based on the manufacturer.

Yes, you can deadlift on a Smith machine, but whether you should depends on your skills and ability.Maietta suggests thinking through the following questions before performing moves on a Smith machine:-How is your range of motion?-Do you have the proper form or mobility to perform these compound moves?If you do not know, Maietta suggests working with a local fitness professional who will be able to help coach you and correct your form if necessary.

Yes, you can build muscle with the consistent use of a Smith machine. Smith machines are considered a good strength and muscle training option for beginners or those without a spotter. However, the drawback is motion is limited to a specific vertical (or slightly angled) path. For sports-specific muscle building, some experts prefer free weight exercises.

Yes, you can squat with a Smith machine. Safety features such as hooks and stoppers can help provide extra protection. Again, be mindful of your abilities and consult with a fitness pro if you are unsure of how to do this safely and with proper form.

#8635. The Lat Training Guide For Building a Stronger and Wider Back

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Most lifters want lats for one reason:  the V-taper. Well-developed lats give your upper body that powerful look from the front, side, and back, and yes, they make T-shirts fit better.

Besides looking awesome, the lats keep your shoulders stable, support better upper-body posture, and connect your arms to your torso, improving form during heavy lifts. Strong lats improve pulling mechanics, create a stronger pressing setup, and help your upper back stay in a better position during squats and deadlifts.

Here we’ll go over all things lats, including:

By the end, you’ll know how to train your lats for a stronger back, better pulls, healthier shoulders, and an upper body that will fill out your T-shirts.

The latissimus dorsi—or lats for short—are the body’s widest muscles and cover much of the back. They’re broad, flat, and fan-shaped, which is why well-developed lats help create that V-Taper look.

Because of their size, the lats attach to the

Because they attach to the upper arm and spine, they influence both shoulder movement and posture.

They also help with scapular depression, which pulls the shoulders down away from your ears and is an important part of good pulling form. Train those actions well, and you’ll build a wider back, stronger pulls, and better control from your shoulders through your hips.

We all know that lats are the engine behind rows, pull-ups, and chin-ups, but some don’t realize the vital role they play beyond them.

During the deadlift, strong, engaged lats help keep the bar close to your body as you pull. When the bar drifts away, the lift gets harder, and your lower back gets unhappy.

Your lats matter during the bench press, too. When engaged, they help create a stable base to press from, improve your pressing path, and transfer force from your leg drive to your upper body.

That is why strong lats aren’t just a “back day” thing: they set the table for better pressing form.

Pulling your lats down and back creates upper-body tightness for barbell back squat. Doing so helps stabilize the bar and keeps you in a stronger, more upright position instead of folding forward into a good morning.

The lats also matter for shoulder health and posture because they influence shoulder position and upper-body alignment. When the lats are balanced in length, they let the shoulder blades rest flat, and the shoulders open back naturally. This supports better posture.

And yes, they matter outside the gym, too. Pulling open heavy doors, climbing, carrying objects close to your body, and lifting things from the floor all involve the lats. Bigger lats create the look, but stronger lats help you pull, brace, carry, and move well.

Because the lats are large and their muscle fibers run in different directions, train them through several pulling paths. You need vertical pulling, horizontal pulling, straight-arm work, loaded stretches, and good form to keep the tension where it belongs.

You know the exercises, but that’s only part of it. For maximum growth and strength, keep these four things in mind.

Progressive Overload: Add load, reps, sets, range of motion, or better control over time. But don’t sacrifice lat tension, shoulder position, or form to move more weight.

Here are general recommendations that work for most lifters most of the time.

Use sets of three to six reps on heavier pulls. Good options include weighted pull-ups, heavy chin-ups, and lat pulldowns. Rest 2 to 3 minutes between sets, and keep the reps clean.

Use sets of eight to 15 reps on pulldowns, rows, dumbbell rows to the hip, seated machine rows, or cable rows. This is your bread-and-butter hypertrophy work. Use a full range of motion, control the stretch, and finish each rep by pulling the elbows toward the ribs or hips, depending on the exercise.

Use sets of 12 to 20 reps on straight-arm pulldowns, kneeling straight-arm pulldowns, cable pullovers, and band straight-arm pulldowns. These are great for lifters who struggle to feel their lats because these exercises isolate them.

Straight-arm pulldown variations are useful before deadlifting because engaging the lats helps maintain a neutral spine and keep the bar close. One or two sets of 10 to 15 reps work well as a primer.

Most lifters can train the lats directly two to three times per week.

Think of 12 to 16 direct lat sets per week as your weekly target. How you divide those sets depends on your goal.

If strength is the priority, spend more sets in the 3 to 6 rep range with weighted pull-ups, heavy pulldowns, chin-ups, and rows. If size is the goal, focus more work in the 8 to 15 rep range with pulldowns, rows, single-arm work, and machine or cable variations. If you struggle to feel your lats, include 12 to 20 rep sets of straight-arm pulldowns, pullovers, or band work.

Here’s an example of how to organize your weekly volume. 12 weekly sets might include four heavier sets, six muscle-building sets, and two higher-rep straight-arm sets. That gives you a fantastic combination of strength, size, and lat connection.

Using too much weight you cannot control might stroke the ego, but it does nothing for your gains. Here are a few more mistakes to watch out for to get the most out of your lat training.

Your hands hold the bar, but your elbows should lead the movement. When lifters focus only on pulling with their hands, chin-ups, pulldowns, and rows often turn into biceps-heavy exercises with a side order of forearm fatigue.

Fix: Drive your elbows down during pulldowns, pull your elbows toward your hips during rows, and tuck your shoulder blades into your back pocket for chin-ups.

Many lifters cut the top of pulldowns, pull-ups, and straight-arm exercises short. That leaves a lot of potential lat tension on the table, because the lats love a loaded stretch.

Fix: Reach overhead or forward under control, keep the ribs down, and feel the stretch without dumping on the shoulder joint. The goal is to control a stretch, not just hang through the connective tissue.

When the ribs flare, the lower back often arches, turning a lat exercise into a lower-back exercise. This can happen during pulldowns, pullovers, and straight-arm work when someone tries to create range they don’t own.

Fix: Keep the ribs stacked over the pelvis by breathing out and bracing the core on top of that. This gives the lats a better chance to lengthen and shorten without the lower back taking over.

If your shoulders shrug toward your ears during rows or pulldowns, your upper traps dominate. Doing so takes the focus off the lats and can lead to upper trap and neck pain.

Fix: Remember to keep your shoulders away from your ears and your chest up. You do this by keeping your neck long.

Lat training has its share of gym myths because everyone wants a wider back. Some advice sounds good until you realize it ignores range of motion, elbow path, body position, and the fact that your biceps will love to steal the show if you let them.

Wide-grip pulldowns and pull-ups are great, but they aren’t magic—and they don’t build wide lats. A wide grip doesn’t automatically increase lat tension. In fact, it often shortens your range of motion, limits the load, and shifts stress to the shoulders and upper back for many lifters. Shoulder-width, medium, and neutral grips offer a longer ROM, and you can lift more weight.

Pull-ups and chin-ups are gold-standard lat builders—but the lats need more. The problem is that pull-ups lock you into a single line of pull. Because the lats are large and wide, with muscle fibers running in different directions, dumbbell and machine variations let you adjust your body position and grips to change the line of pull and target muscle fibers that chin-ups miss.

Rows hammer the upper back, but they can also hit the lats with the right setup, grip, and elbow path. Rowing high with flared elbows shifts more attention to the traps, rear delts, and upper back. Rowing back toward the hip with your elbow close gives the lats more work.

They assist with deadlifts, squats, bench press setup, posture, and shoulder control. So yes, train them for width. But don’t forget they also help you lift better when no one is admiring your V-taper.

The lats don’t need a separate “back day or bust” approach. You can train them hard during an upper-body session or weave them into a full-body workout.

Goal: Build lat size and strength while still training the chest, shoulders, upper back, and arms.

Goal: Train the lats as part of a full-body workout.

The winning formula is this: Train the lats with vertical pulls, rows, straight-arm work, single-arm variations, and exercises that challenge the stretch position. Keep the ribs down, control the shoulders, pull toward the hips to engage more lats, and stop letting your biceps, traps, and lower back take over.

Remember to lock the lats in during your squat, bench, and deadlift because they are the difference between a sloppy rep and a clean one. Use enough volume to grow and enough weight to build muscle and strength, but never shortchange the range of motion.

If you do it right, you’ll need to buy larger shirts.

#8634. After Training for My First Marathon, I Felt Like My Body Didn’t Look Like the Runner I Thought I’d Become. Experts Helped Me See Otherwise.

Marathon training changed how I saw my body—even when it didn’t change how I looked.

Two weeks out from my first marathon, I looked in the mirror and didn’t see the version of myself I thought I would. There was no six-pack, not even a hint of ab definition. My glutes weren’t particularly sculpted, and I wouldn’t exactly describe myself as lean like many runners I see.

At 5-foot-10, I’ve never been the smallest girl in the room. And while my long legs certainly help me cover more distance, I expected months of marathon training to leave me looking more visibly athletic, with more muscle definition and a physique that reflected just how hard I’d been working. I thought that after months of early alarms, added protein, and steadily increasing mileage, I’d look in the mirror and see a different body type.

Somewhere along the way, I absorbed the idea that a runner’s body should look a certain way. When mine didn’t match that image, I started wondering if I wasn’t training hard enough, if I was doing something wrong, or if my body simply wasn’t responding the way it was supposed to.

As I approached race day, I thought about why I was holding myself to that standard in the first place, especially because I was running the New York City Marathon on behalf of Planned Parenthood of Greater New York, an organization whose work centers on bodily autonomy and compassionate care.

Why was I putting so much pressure on my body to look different when it was already doing something incredible? I realized training for a marathon isn’t just about building endurance; it can also mean confronting the expectations you place on yourself.

So many people have an idea of what a “runner’s body” is supposed to look like, particularly fed by what we see online. When you see the same body type represented over and over, it’s easy to start associating that appearance with athleticism. But running a marathon is an enormous physical undertaking, and there’s no single body type that proves you’re capable of doing it.

Clinical sport psychologist Hillary Cauthen, PsyD, explains that the concept of “a runner’s body” is “largely a socially constructed ideal influenced by media representation, sport culture, and the tendency to associate certain physical characteristics with athletic success.” She adds that distance running has historically been represented by a lean body type, particularly smaller-framed athletes, which can leave some recreational runners questioning whether they fit the mold.

Comparison is a large part of this problem, too, says Cindra Kamphoff, PhD, mental performance coach and founder of the Mentally Strong Institute. “We see elite runners and start believing that’s what we should look like,” she explains.

Marathon training is practically a master class in comparison, making it hard to avoid. You’re tracking your pace, watching your mileage climb, sharing runs on Strava, and seeing what everyone else is doing. It can feel like your body should be changing right alongside your stats.

There’s also a particularly frustrating point of tension for women, who can feel caught between the cultural expectation to be smaller and the athletic ideal of looking lean and strong. Carinthia Bank, LCSW, a social worker who works with runners on body image, describes this as the “female athlete paradox,” in which women are judged against both ideals.

For example, a woman might recognize that building strength and fueling adequately are essential to marathon training, yet still feel pressure to maintain a smaller frame or worry that eating more to support her mileage will change her body in ways she doesn’t want. These competing expectations can shape how women judge their bodies, even as they get stronger and more capable, Bank explains.

Marathon training can also increase the time we spend thinking about our bodies, particularly when we’re experiencing physical or emotional discomfort, Bank adds. Many runners tend to think they’d feel better if their bodies were different, which can lead to judgment and blame toward the body they have.

That’s the trap I found myself in. While I was training for 26.2 miles, part of me was still measuring my progress against an imaginary finish line where I’d emerge with a completely different-looking body. I would accomplish something I’d never done before, like running my farthest distance, yet I was using my appearance to dictate my progress.

Cauthen offers a simple definition to keep in mind: “A runner’s body is not a specific shape or size. It is a body that runs.”

Here’s the thing about marathon training: Your body adapts to the physical demands of running, but those changes don’t guarantee an aesthetic transformation. You might build muscle, experience weight fluctuations, or notice an increase in appetite as your body works to fuel and recover. “Improved fitness does not always result in weight loss or a smaller body,” Cauthen says.

There’s also a practical reason not to make getting smaller one of your goals in marathon training. Kamphoff encourages runners “to focus on fueling for performance rather than restricting for appearance,” reminding us that “you can’t expect your body to perform at its best if you’re constantly trying to make it take up less space.”

Marathon training requires substantial energy, and restricting food to change your appearance can leave you without enough fuel to support your workouts and recovery.

Plus, fixating on your size can affect more than physical performance. “Focusing on getting smaller can distract and discourage us from actions that are helpful to performance and mental health,” Bank says. When you’re preoccupied with changing your body, you can miss out on learning what helps you perform, enjoying the process, and appreciating everything your body allows you to do.

I had to confront the fact that I’d been treating my appearance as a report card for my training. If I was working hard enough, I assumed I’d eventually see visible proof in the mirror. But I realized I can become a stronger, more capable runner without looking the way I imagined I would.

For me, that meant recognizing that the body I’d been criticizing was the same one carrying me through early morning runs and increasingly long distances. My body wasn’t failing at becoming a runner’s body—I’d been expecting it to meet a standard that had very little to do with what I was asking it to do.

I wish I could say that learning all of this made me instantly love every inch of my body, but that wouldn’t be honest. I’m still working on it, and I still have moments when I catch my reflection and wonder why I don’t look the way I imagined I would after months of training. But I’m trying to shift my focus from what my body looks like to what it’s allowing me to do, with the help of these expert tips.

“One of the most important shifts runners can make is moving from body evaluation to body appreciation,” Cauthen says. Instead of asking whether I look like someone who runs marathons, I’m trying to ask myself what my body has helped me accomplish. And the answer is a lot more impressive than whether or not I have visible abs.

As I got closer to race day, I continued to remind myself that I don’t have to look a certain way to feel proud of what I accomplished. My body carried me through months of training, and that’s worth celebrating all on its own.

I’m also learning to give myself a little more grace when my expectations don’t match reality. Bank reminds runners that “human beings usually get uncomfortable when there’s a difference between what we wanted and what we get,” and encourages compassion rather than self-criticism.

I don’t have to ignore the fact that I expected marathon training to change my appearance, but I also don’t want those expectations to overshadow everything else I’ve gained, including running farther than I ever thought possible, learning how to fuel and maintain energy, and showing up for myself.

Cauthen recommends distinguishing between observing a physical change and assigning a negative meaning to it, which has really stuck with me. “Noticing that your legs have become more muscular, your weight has fluctuated, or your clothing fits differently is an observation,” she explains. “Deciding those changes mean you are too big, not fit enough, or don’t look like a runner is an interpretation.” This helped me realize how quickly I can turn a neutral observation into self-criticism.

Instead of jumping to conclusions, Cauthen says it’s helpful to ask yourself a few questions when those negative thoughts creep in. For example, “is this thought based on evidence or comparison?” and “am I evaluating my body based on appearance or how I feel and function?” These questions challenge the assumptions that we tend to make about our bodies.

Kamphoff encourages runners to develop what she calls an “inner coach” instead of listening to an inner critic. One strategy she recommends is to “capture your wins” by writing down three things you’re proud of after training. The idea is to shift your attention from perceived imperfections to the progress you’ve made.

I’m trying to practice this by celebrating the things that don’t show up in a mirror. For example, I’ve learned how to pace myself and keep going when a run gets uncomfortable. “Your body has been showing up for you mile after mile. Make sure your self-talk is showing up for your body, too,” says Kamphoff.

Ultimately, I’m learning that I don’t need to love how my body looks every single day to respect what it does for me. “Body acceptance does not require loving every part of your appearance every day,” Cauthen says. “Sometimes it starts with respecting your body’s needs and appreciating its efforts, even when your feelings about your appearance are complicated.”

I can have complicated feelings about the way I look and still be proud of the athlete I’ve become. And I can show up at the starting line without meeting some imaginary physical standard first.

That’s the mindset I carried with me to the marathon. I ran 26.2 miles for a cause I believe in, after months of training that challenged me physically and mentally. My body didn’t have to look a certain way to deserve that moment.

After all those early mornings and hours of preparation, I finally crossed the finish line, put the medal around my neck, and walked out of Central Park feeling something I hadn’t quite felt throughout training: pride. Not because my body looked different, but because of everything it had just done. I felt so grateful for my legs that kept moving, my strength that carried me through the tough miles, and a body that got me to the finish line without injury.

No, my body may not have looked like the “marathon body” I once imagined, but it was a marathon body. I didn’t need a mirror selfie to prove what I’d accomplished: I ran all 26.2 miles. Honestly, what could be more impressive than that?

Alyssa is a New York City–based runner and lifestyle writer covering the intersection of fitness, beauty, and everyday routines. Currently training for the NYC Marathon, she brings a firsthand perspective to stories on endurance, recovery, and the mental side of running—alongside the real-life habits that support it. Her work is rooted in what’s practical, personal, and worth incorporating into your own routine.

#8632. Weini Kelati Has Taken a One-Mile at a Time Approach for Taking On the NYC Marathon

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

There was a time when eight miles felt like an eternity to Weini Kelati. Now, toward the tail end of preparing for her first full marathon, she can find herself 10 miles into a 20-mile workout and realize the distance that once signaled the end of a hard day has now become the halfway point.

This progression says a lot about what marathon preparation requires. The obvious difference between a half marathon and 26.2 miles is distance, but Kelati discovered that building a marathon body involved more than adding more miles to her workload. The body must be conditioned to tolerate additional volume, know how to fuel, how to recover, and eventually trust that the work was enough when fatigue arrives.

Kelati, the American half-marathon record holder, Olympian, and five-time national champion will make her marathon debut at the TCS New York City Marathon on Nov. 1. Speaking with Muscle & Fitness through New York Road Runners, she explained that she had always seen the half marathon as a gateway toward eventually racing 26.2, even giving herself a loose requirement of completing four or five before considering making the move.

“I think first I was nervous,” Kelati said. “I was like, ‘Oh my goodness. This is going to be hard because I used to be at low mileage.’”

What surprised her most isn’t how difficult the transition was, but how quickly the human body can begin adjusting to something once intimidating as simply another day in training.

During Kelati’s half-marathon preparation, she said her highest weekly mileage reached around 75 miles. For this build, she knew that number would have to climb into the 90s. The increase initially made her nervous. Once she started, however, something unexpected happened: She began enjoying it.

The biggest adjustment was redefining what constitutes a long effort. In the lead-up to a 10K or half-marathon, a six- or eight-mile tempo run could represent one of the bigger sustained sessions on her schedule. Marathon preparation introduced two different types of long runs, including easier road efforts and workouts, which she can cover approximately 20 miles at a specific pace.

“I’m not the type of person who rushes into something,” Kelati said. “I always take a lot baby steps to get used to something.”

That patience allowed her body to establish a new baseline without making every unfamiliar distance feel like a test. Her weekly structure wasn’t radically different from half-marathon training, either. The biggest change is that familiar paces and workouts extended further, asking her to sustain what she already knew for considerably longer.

The result was a changed internal relationship with distance.

“When you get to eight miles, you start saying, ‘Oh, I’m already halfway,’ instead of saying, ‘Oh, I used to stop here,” Kelati says. “The mind and the body change the way I have to handle it.”

The added mileage exposed an area Kelati admits hasn’t always been a strength for her: nutrition.

At shorter distances, she could get away with habits that weren’t conducive with marathon preparation. For years, she could wake up and run without eating anything because consuming food before a morning session wasn’t something she enjoyed.

The marathon build forced her to adjust that part of her routine. When there is a large increase in workload, personal preferences eventually run into physical necessity.

“You have to help the body as much as it’s working,” Kelati said. “During the marathon training, you have to fuel your body. You have to get ready for the next hard run.”

She learned that fueling for her bigger sessions didn’t mean forcing down a huge meal. If appetite was an issue, she would have smaller meals spaced throughout the day. This same logic changed her behavior after a run.

Meals were the common recovery method for Kelati,  but the increased workload led her to incorporate recovery drinks and pay closer attention to getting nutrition back into her body sooner.

Kelati’s favorite recovery method didn’t require scheduling or involve any expensive equipment.

“I love taking naps after every single run,” she said. “It doesn’t matter how hard or easy the run I do, I just have to take a little nap every day and, of course, more than eight hours of sleep during the night.”

Kelati fully believes giving her body adequate downtime has been an important reason she was able to absorb demanding training and be able to show up the following morning and ask her body to perform again.

There is one part of marathon preparation Kelati couldn’t completely simulate.

She could run 20 miles in training, nap after training, and ask experienced marathoners what waits beyond the distances she already knows.

Until New York, however, she won’t know exactly how her own body and mind will respond to racing 26.2 miles. That uncertainty doesn’t seem to bother her as much as thinking about the entire distance at once.

“I don’t like counting the miles,” Kelati said. “It seems pretty long for me to think about it while you’re standing on the start line or you just started. You’re in the first mile, and you’re just like, ‘Oh, we have like 25 miles to go.’”

Instead, she intends on remaining completely in the moment.

“I just like to be in the present and focus one mile at a time,” she said.

Insights have helped. Kelati did the same thing before moving into half marathons, quizzing runners about which points of the race are the most challenging so she could have some idea of what awaited her. This time, the answer is a different number.

“They keep saying, ‘You’re going to start racing when you get to 30K,’” she says. “It can be different, but also it’ll give you what to expect or what’s coming when you get to that distance and how you’re going to handle it.”

Discomfort will eventually arrive, and Kelati’s strategy is a simple one. She reminds herself that the pain is temporary and that she’d rather find out what she’s capable of than finish wondering whether she would have given more.

It’s a mindset that comes from weeks of watching her body handle workloads she once was uncertain about. Kelati says one of the things she’s most proud of during this build has been how naturally she adapted to the training her coach put in front of her. Each completed run and training session has chipped away the stone of uncertainty that existed when 26.2 was still just a thought.

“When you try to do something new, you always have these thoughts that can prevent you from doing something,” Kelati said. “But then once you just start doing it, I feel like we can do anything when we believe.”

When Kelati reaches the start line in Staten Island, there will be lots of thoughts in her head. All the early morning runs, how well she’s done in races in New York, and all the months spent gradually extending what her body can tolerate.

She will let those thoughts flow. Her goal for that morning speaks to her readiness.

“I want to feel good just standing there and say, ‘Today is a great day,’” Kelati said. ‘“I feel good. Let’s do this.’”

My friend Sean Mullaney, the FI Tax Guy, recently published an interesting article about the potential downsides of annuities. One of his observations is so simple that I think it's easy to overlook:

Most Americans already have an annuity. It's called Social Security.

Think about what an annuity is trying to accomplish. You give up some control over a pool of money in exchange for a predictable stream of income, often for the rest of your life. Social Security already provides lifetime income, with the added benefit of inflation adjustments.

For a married couple receiving substantial Social Security benefits, that could represent tens of thousands of dollars of annual income that they don't have to generate by selling investments.

#8628. JASON AVELAR AND GARRETT BEAL SHARE THE STORY OF PRESCOTT JUNIOR HIGH’S LEGACY OF PHYSICAL EDUCATION EXCELLENCE

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

President Donald Trump announced the re-establishment and restoration of the Presidential Fitness Test on July 31, 2025, when he signed an Executive Order revitalizing the test along with the President’s Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition. Since then, the Trump administration also announced the Presidential Fitness School Innovation Challenge, a competition which invites “schools, districts, and youth-serving organizations to design and execute creative, repeatable models that inspire student participation, teamwork, and enthusiasm for the Presidential Fitness Test (PFT).”

One school that could serve as an example for others to follow and may be a top contender should they enter that challenge would be Prescott Junior High School in Modesto, California. The school overall has a great reputation, but it is best known for their P.E. program. Current teachers Jason Avelar and Garrett Beal are two of the teachers for this program, but its legacy as a fitness-focused juggernaut goes back nearly a half-century.

Beal, who also served as a police officer for a period of his life, played sports as a kid but credited a high school wrestling coach for introducing him to the weight room.

“It was the first sport where I saw that being strong helped,” he said. “I fell in love even more with fitness than wrestling.”

Avelar was bitten by the iron bug while playing football in his high school days but also found he had natural leadership skills as a linebacker. His coaches confirmed this and could have played a role in him becoming a gym teacher.

“I had a few coaches and teachers pull me aside and said, ‘Hey, I think you’d be a great teacher.’”

Both Beal and Alevar are reminded often about the history they are a part of. Modeled closely after the La Sierra High School Physical Education Program (the famous 1960s President’s Council on Physical Fitness model) Prescott’s program has challenged junior high students for decades using a high-standard and military-inspired structure.

In 1973, then Prescott P.E. teacher Mark Wilson saw a demonstration of a high-intensity, physical fitness-based curriculum. Wilson was inspired by the concept and used his own version on his students, challenging them to make fitness a priority at an early age.

There is a color and points based system to help gauge the students’ progress and motivate them to work harder. All students start with zero points and white trunks, and there are 20 different fitness tests. Each test offers one, two, or four points for their performances. Once a student achieves 60 points, they earn red trunks. However, the scoring goes back to zero because they are at a new level with harder challenges. Once they work back up to 60 points, they then earn blue trunks.

“The tests at that point get very challenging,” Avelar said. There are also gold and purple trunks for those students that do very well in the program. Prescott even has a P.E. Hall of Fame, where students can be recognized. Avelar acknowledged one student who even cleared the purple trunk scoring early, meaning they had to create a new level just for her.

“We decided on custom trunks. Once you pass purple, you get to pick your own.”

The bars may be seen as super high for some, but Avelar and Beal share that either students rise to the occasion and reach it, or they get closer than they may have had there not been that high bar in the first place.

The results speak for themselves. One student ran two miles in 12 minutes, 27 seconds. Another performed over 6,000 continuous sit-ups, and multiple students have reportedly performed over 1,000 unbroken pushups. The Prescott program has had a generational impact in Modesto.

Beal said, “I wear my Prescott shirt anywhere around town, and people stop to talk to me about when they went there.” He even met one man at a book club, and he recognized the last name on their Hall of Fame wall.

Other teachers at Prescott were also students there, and both Beal and Avelar confirmed that they strive to be the best examples possible by making their wellness a priority. They also said that even though the high school P.E. programs may not have as intense of programs, the students who went to Prescott continue their fitness journeys after they move on. Others may take the school for granted but realize what they were a part of later on.

Avelar said, “As they leave, they realize ‘Oh crap, this is a super special place.’”

Both teachers take great pride in not only what they are a part of but having added their own chapters to the Prescott story. They are reminded of how important their work is every day, and they definitely don’t take the positions they are in for granted.

Avelar stated. “The fulfillment I get from showing up to school every day and seeing kids reach their goals, push themselves, do things they’ve never done before, and seeing the excitement on their faces is why I do it.”

Beal added, “This is such a special place to be,”

There is no official word on how many schools will enter the Presidential Fitness School Innovation Challenge, but both Avelar and Beal were pleased that the Presidential Fitness Test has been reinstated, and they hope that it can serve as a catalyst for other P.E. programs to do more to help their students embrace fitness, pushing themselves, and taking on great challenges. As they have seen first hand, the impact goes beyond the school walls and can last for many years to come.

To learn more about the PFT or the School Innovation Challenge, go to fitness.gov.

You can follow the Prescott program on Instagram @prescott_standard and Beal and Alevar on LinkedIn.

M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins contributed to this Fit to Serve article.
